ety.text: From Middle English waden, from Old English wadan, from Proto-West Germanic *wadan, from Proto-Germanic *wadaną (“to go, pass through”), from Proto-Indo-European *weh₂dʰ- (“to go”). Cognates include Saterland Frisian waadje (“to wade”), West Frisian wâdzje (“to wade”), Dutch waden (“to wade”), German Low German waden (“to wade”), German waten (“to wade”), Danish vade (“to wade”), Swedish vada (“to wade”), Icelandic vaða (“to wade”), and Latin vādō (“go, walk; rush”).

senses.d: To walk through water or something that impedes progress.
ex: So eagerly the fiend […] / With head, hands, wings, or feet, pursues his way, / And swims, or sinks, or wades, or creeps, or flies.
to wade through a dull book
And wades through fumes, and gropes his way.

senses.d: To walk through (water or similar impediment); to pass through by wading.
To gleam intermittently through clouds or mist.
ex: ... the pale light of a crescent moon wading among the black and lowering clouds.
It's rain afoor meeght, t'sun waded sadly ez sha peeped ower Roseberry.
to wade into a fight or a debate
We had to be careful during our dangerous wade across the river.

senses.d: A ford; a place to cross a river.

grp.label: to walk through water or something that impedes progress

ety.text: From guado + -are, possibly corresponding to Late Latin vadāre, from Latin vadum, but influenced by Germanic into a Vulgar Latin form *uadāre. Compare French guéer.
Ancient Greek -ῐ́ζω (-ĭ́zō)bor. Latin -izāre Spanish -ear Spanish vadear From vado + -ear.
Italian sguazzarebor. Spanish esguazar Borrowed from Italian sguazzare.

pt:vadear.gl: to ford; to wade (to walk through a body of water)
